damon-self-ligating-braces.summary: Self-ligating braces that hold the wire with a sliding clip, used to align teeth and broaden the arch for a straighter, fuller smile.

quick.overview:
Damon braces are orthodontic brackets that hold the archwire with a built-in sliding door instead of rubber ties. People choose them for straighter teeth and a broader, fuller-looking smile, and the system is marketed for expanding the arch without extractions.

The passive clip lets the wire slide with little friction, so teeth move under lighter forces as the wire shape guides alignment. Systematic reviews describe lower friction as the most consistent advantage, with mixed findings on treatment time, comfort and hygiene. Looksmax forum users credit the system with arch expansion and, in some posts, jaw changes; no trials show facial-bone change from the bracket type.
quick.how: Treatment is run by an orthodontist as a standard course of braces: brackets bonded to the teeth, a series of archwires, and regular adjustment visits over many months. Users typically pair it with a retainer afterwards to hold the result.
quick.risks: Risks are those of braces generally: tooth soreness, mouth irritation, decalcification or decay if cleaning is poor, and relapse without a retainer. Reviews do not link the bracket type to extra hygiene problems. Claims of jaw or maxilla change have not been studied.

angle.text: The payoff people want is a straighter, fuller smile. Self-ligating brackets move the teeth under light forces, broadening the arch and aligning them, and forum users credit the system with extra arch expansion. Reviews report lower friction as the main documented advantage.

teeth-whitening-pens.summary: Portable brush-on whitening gel pens that lift surface stains for a brighter smile at home.

quick.overview:
Whitening pens are brush-on gel applicators that people use to brighten their smile at home, as a convenient alternative to strips or trays. The result is a lighter-looking tooth surface as stains lift.

The gel, often peroxide-based, breaks down stain molecules on and in enamel when painted onto the tooth. Research specific to pens comes from laboratory studies of peroxide penetration, enamel effects and filling colour; no human trials of pens were found.
quick.how: The gel is brushed onto dry teeth, usually once or twice a day over a stretch of days or weeks, and the pen is small enough to carry for touch-ups. Users often use it between other whitening treatments or alongside whitening toothpaste.
quick.risks: Peroxide whiteners can cause tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, and may affect enamel texture and tooth-coloured fillings, which do not whiten. Allowed peroxide strengths differ by region: EU retail products may contain up to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, while the US FDA endorses gels below 6 percent.

angle.text: Users reach for whitening pens as a portable way to brighten their smile between other treatments. Peroxide gel brushed on the teeth lifts surface stains, so teeth look slightly lighter. Evidence on pens specifically comes from laboratory studies.

peroxycarboxylic-pap-whitening.summary: A peroxide-free whitening agent (PAP) used to lighten teeth, studied in one small laser-activated trial.

quick.overview:
PAP (phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid) is a non-peroxide whitening agent sold in some whitening products as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide. People want lighter teeth with less of the sensitivity associated with peroxide.

A peroxycarboxylic acid applied to the teeth oxidises stain compounds, and it can be activated by light or laser. Published human data is one 2025 study of fifteen patients with mild to moderate stains using an 810-nm diode laser.
quick.how: It is applied to the teeth as a gel or similar product, sometimes with light or laser activation in a clinic setting, and used in place of peroxide whitening. Users typically run it as a short course and compare shade before and after.
quick.risks: Safety and sensitivity data are limited to that small study, and no long-term data were found. As with any whitening product, tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the main things to watch for.

angle.text: PAP is promoted as a peroxide-free way to get lighter teeth with less sensitivity. The agent oxidises stain compounds on the teeth, optionally boosted by light or laser. The published support is one small 2025 laser-activated study of fifteen patients.

vita-shade-guide.summary: The A1-D4 tooth-colour scale dentists use to name how light teeth are and track whitening results.

quick.overview:
The VITA shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs labelled A1 to D4 that puts a number on how light or dark teeth are. People use it to record a starting shade and see how far whitening has moved it.

A clinician holds tabs next to the tooth and picks the closest match by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity); instruments can also measure colour. Dental studies have examined its limits, including colour coverage gaps and differences between visual and instrument readings. In appearance communities, shade numbers serve as shorthand for how white teeth are.
quick.how: A dentist or the user compares tabs to the teeth in consistent lighting before whitening, then again afterwards to see the change. It is combined with whitening treatments, and photos are often taken alongside the shade.
quick.risks: The guide itself carries no risk because it is a measurement reference, not a treatment. Visual matching accuracy varies with lighting and the person doing the match.

angle.text: Dentists and whitening-focused users use the VITA scale to put a number on how light teeth are before and after treatment. Tabs from A1 to D4 are matched to the tooth, so progress can be tracked. It is a measurement reference rather than a treatment and is widely used in cosmetic dentistry.

temporal-brow-lift.summary: Surgical lift of the outer eyebrow through temple incisions, used to raise a drooping brow tail and open the eye area.

quick.overview:
A temporal brow lift raises the outer part of the eyebrow through incisions hidden in the hair-bearing temple area. Patients seek it to lift a drooping brow tail and open the eye area, and looksmaxxing communities group it with eye-area surgery.

Tissue at the brow tail is released and re-fixed higher at the temple, by subcutaneous, endoscopic or combined methods. The lift is visible after surgery and is documented in surgical case series and technique comparisons; surgeons disagree about the best approach.
quick.how: It is done by a plastic or facial surgeon, usually under anaesthesia, sometimes combined with eyelid surgery. Swelling and bruising settle over a couple of weeks, and the brow position is judged once healing is done.
quick.risks: Reported risks include injury to the frontal branch of the facial nerve, numbness, hair loss at the incisions, infection, bleeding and recurrence of brow drop with some methods.

angle.text: People want a lifted outer brow and a more open eye area. Surgeons release tissue at the brow tail and fix it higher at the temple through hidden incisions. The lift is visible after healing and is documented in surgical series.

cheek-lift.summary: Surgical repositioning of sagging cheek tissue to give a fuller, more lifted midface, studied mainly in ageing faces.

quick.overview:
A cheek lift, or midface lift, moves sagging cheek tissue and the malar fat pad upward for a fuller, more youthful midface. Some younger men who feel their cheeks look flat or hollow discuss it for a more defined look.

Surgeons lift the cheek soft tissue, sometimes beneath the periosteum, through incisions at the lower eyelid, hairline or inside the mouth, and fix it higher. Published results come mostly from surgeon-authored technique series on ageing faces, often combined with eyelid surgery or a facelift; use in young men has not been studied.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon, often as part of a wider facial rejuvenation plan. Milder cases are sometimes approached with non-surgical options such as threads, fillers or energy-based devices. Recovery involves swelling and bruising over weeks.
quick.risks: Listed complications include haematoma, nerve injury, scarring and eyelid malposition; smoking raises the risk of skin necrosis. Results are documented mainly in surgeon-authored series rather than controlled trials.

angle.text: People want a fuller, higher midface instead of flat or sagging cheeks. Surgeons reposition the cheek soft tissue and malar fat pad upward and fix it there. The studies concern ageing faces; use in young men is discussed in forums.

facial-feminization-surgery.summary: A set of bone and soft-tissue facial operations developed for transgender women, now eyed by some looksmaxxers for brow, nose and cheek work.

quick.overview:
Facial feminization surgery is a group of operations that soften masculine facial features: lowering the hairline, reshaping the brow ridge, nose and lips, building up the cheeks, and reducing the chin, jaw and Adam's apple. The aim is a more harmonious face with softer features.

It was developed from the early 1980s by Douglas Ousterhout for transgender women. Systematic reviews report improved quality of life and a low complication rate, though the evidence is mostly case series. On looksmax.org some users discuss borrowing its brow, nose and cheek techniques for male faces; that use has not been studied.
quick.how: Surgeons plan from CT and MRI imaging, then reshape bone, move soft tissue and add cheek volume with implants or fat. The work may be staged or combined into one long operation, with recovery measured in weeks.
quick.risks: Reported risks include nerve injury, infection, implant displacement, fat resorption, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and voice changes after Adam's apple reduction. These are major operations under general anaesthesia; costs can be high and coverage depends on country and insurer.

angle.text: The payoff is a face with softer, more harmonious features, with the brow, nose, cheeks and jaw reshaped. Surgeons work on bone and soft tissue, so changes are visible after healing. Developed for transgender women, it is also discussed in forums for male faces.

zygomatic-reduction.summary: Surgery that shaves or repositions the cheekbones to narrow the face, popular in Asian aesthetic surgery.

quick.overview:
Zygomatic reduction, also called malarplasty or cheekbone shaving, reshapes or repositions the cheekbones to give a narrower or flatter midface. People with a wide or prominent midface seek it for a slimmer facial width.

The cheek bone is cut and reshaped or moved inward, as forum posters describe it; some say shaving mainly reduces forward projection rather than width. On looksmax.org users debate whether width comes from bone or fat and whether the surgery improves proportions. The wiki's sources contain no outcome studies.
quick.how: It is a surgical procedure done under anaesthesia by a facial or plastic surgeon, popular in Asian aesthetic surgery. Swelling settles over weeks, and the final shape is judged after healing.
quick.risks: It is a bone-cutting operation under anaesthesia. Forum members report results ranging from very good to very bad, and no complication data were available in the sources used here.

angle.text: People with a wide or prominent midface want a narrower, slimmer facial width. The cheekbone is shaved or repositioned inward, so the change is visible after healing. Forum members report mixed before-and-after outcomes.

serdev-suture.summary: A needle-suture thread lifting method that holds sagging facial tissue higher for a tighter-looking face.

quick.overview:
The Serdev suture is a thread-lift technique in which sutures are placed under the skin to hold sagging tissue up, rather than cutting skin out. It is associated with a surgeon named Serdev and belongs to the suspension-thread family of minimally invasive lifts.

Suture threads placed in the dermis and subcutis anchor lax tissue in a higher position for a tighter-looking face. A 2016 review of suspension threads notes that Serdev introduced a polycaproamide suture; published evidence on this specific needle method is thin.
quick.how: It is done by a trained practitioner as an in-office or minor-surgery procedure, as a lower-downtime alternative to a facelift. Results are visible once placed.
quick.risks: The 2016 review reports that early sutures increased inflammatory reaction. General references note that threads can be difficult to remove and that practitioner training varies.

angle.text: People want a tighter, lifted face without a full facelift. Needle sutures anchor sagging facial tissue in a higher position, and the lift is visible when placed. Published evidence on this specific technique is thin.

facial-autologous-muscular-injection-fam.summary: A fat-grafting variant that places a patient's own fat into facial muscle to restore volume and contour.

quick.overview:
FAMI is a facial fat-grafting approach in which a person's own fat is injected into facial muscle to restore volume and contour, giving a fuller, more contoured face. A 2007 review lists it with lipostructure and facial fat rebalancing as newer concepts for three-dimensional rejuvenation of the whole face.

Fat is harvested from elsewhere on the body and injected into facial muscle, as the name describes. Little else is published on it specifically, and the same review notes that practical ways to measure fat-transfer outcomes objectively are lacking.
quick.how: It is a clinic procedure done by a surgeon, with fat taken from one area of the body and placed in the face. Swelling settles over days to weeks, and part of the fat may be reabsorbed before the final result.
quick.risks: General fat-grafting references list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularities, infection and partial reabsorption of the fat. FAMI-specific safety data were not found.

angle.text: The payoff is restored volume and a fuller, more contoured face using the patient's own fat. Fat is harvested and injected into facial muscle. A 2007 review lists it among newer fat-transfer concepts, and little is published on it specifically.

babyliss-trimmers-stylers.summary: Clippers and trimmers from a French-origin brand for keeping haircuts, fades and beard lines sharp at home.

quick.overview:
BaByliss makes hair dryers, straighteners, curling irons, clippers and beard trimmers; the brand began in France in 1960 and has been owned by Conair since 1995. Users reach for its clippers and trimmers to keep haircuts, fades, beard edges and necklines sharp and even at home.

Clippers and trimmers cut with two close-fitting blades, one moving sideways against the other, driven by a motor. The cleaner lines are visible immediately. No appearance-outcome studies exist for the brand.
quick.how: Users run clippers with guards for length and a trimmer for edging and outlines, usually every week or so to keep lines crisp. They are often paired with a beard routine or a regular fade.
quick.risks: No safety data on specific models were available. A general reference notes blades need lubrication and that ceramic blades can break. Nicks and skin irritation are possible with close trimming.

angle.text: Users reach for BaByliss clippers and trimmers to keep haircuts, fades, beard edges and necklines tidy at home. The blades give sharper, even lines that are visible immediately, for a cleaner and more polished look.

remington-ipl-home-device.summary: Remington's home IPL flasher that reduces body and facial hair over repeated sessions on light-to-medium skin.

quick.overview:
Remington sells home intense pulsed light (IPL) devices under its iLight line, used to thin out body or facial hair over repeated sessions as an alternative to shaving or clinic treatment. The goal is smoother, less hairy skin.

Melanin in the hair absorbs the broad-spectrum light and heats the follicle; only hairs in the growth phase respond, so sessions are repeated. IPL has been studied in clinic systems and the home category on lighter skin; trials of this specific device were not found.
quick.how: Users flash the device over shaved skin in repeated sessions over weeks, then taper to occasional maintenance. It works best on darker hair, and the manufacturer limits use to light-to-medium skin tones.
quick.risks: Burns, redness and pigment changes are reported with light-based hair removal. The manufacturer limits use to lighter skin tones, and eye protection matters with any IPL device.

angle.text: People use the Remington iLight at home to thin body or facial hair over repeated sessions. Light heats the hair follicles, so fewer hairs regrow and skin looks smoother. IPL is studied on light-to-medium skin; trials of this specific device are not found.

veet-depilatory-cream.summary: Hair-dissolving cream that leaves skin smooth within minutes, with hair regrowing in days.

quick.overview:
Veet is a mass-market depilatory brand whose creams dissolve the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. People use it on arms, legs, chest or other areas for smooth skin within minutes, without a razor.

Thioglycolate salts in a high-pH base break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, softening the shaft until it wipes away. The follicle is left intact, so hair regrows within days. No clinical trials of the creams were found.
quick.how: The cream is spread over the area, left for the time on the label, then wiped or rinsed off. Users repeat it every few days as hair grows back, and many use it as an alternative to shaving or waxing.
quick.risks: Irritation and chemical burns are possible with alkaline depilatories, and labels advise patch testing. A 2002 case series linked Veet wax strips, not creams, to allergic contact dermatitis.

angle.text: Users apply Veet to leave arms, legs, chest or other areas smooth within minutes, without a razor. The cream dissolves hair keratin so the hair wipes off at the surface. The smooth result is visible immediately and hair typically regrows within days.

nair-depilatory.summary: Classic drugstore depilatory cream that dissolves body hair at the surface for smooth skin that regrows in days.

quick.overview:
Nair is a long-running chemical hair remover, launched in 1940 and now owned by Church & Dwight, sold in women's and men's lines. People use it to remove body hair quickly without shaving and get smooth skin straight away.

Thioglycolate or calcium hydroxide breaks the disulfide bonds in hair keratin so the hair can be wiped off at the surface. The follicle is left intact, so hair grows back. No brand-specific clinical studies were found.
quick.how: The cream, lotion or spray is applied to the area, left for the label time, then wiped off and rinsed. Users commonly repeat it every few days as hair regrows.
quick.risks: Harsh actives can irritate skin and labels advise patch testing. No brand-specific safety studies were found.

angle.text: Nair is a long-standing drugstore way to remove body hair quickly without shaving. The cream breaks down hair keratin and the hair wipes away at the surface, leaving smooth skin straight away. Users commonly repeat it every few days as hair regrows.

manscaped-trimmers.summary: Electric body trimmers marketed for men's grooming, shortening and tidying body hair for a neater look.

quick.overview:
Manscaped sells electric trimmers aimed at male body and below-the-belt grooming, led by the Lawn Mower trimmer. Users shorten and tidy hair without fully removing it, for a neater, groomed look that is visible immediately.

Rotary or foil blades cut hair at skin level, with guards for length. The brand, founded in San Diego in 2016, is known for humour-driven advertising, and critics cite premium pricing and guard durability. No clinical studies were found.
quick.how: Users trim with a guard to set length, or without one for a closer cut, on a regular schedule as hair grows back. It is often used alongside a shower and moisturiser routine.
quick.risks: Nicks or irritation are generally possible with body trimming. Reviews cited for the brand raise pricing and trim-guard durability concerns.

angle.text: Manscaped trimmers let users shorten and tidy body hair without fully removing it. Blades cut hair at skin level, with guards for length, and the trimmed result is visible immediately for a neater, groomed look.

electric-tweezers.summary: Battery-powered pluckers for brows and stray hair, some sold with a claim that an electric pulse keeps hair away longer.

quick.overview:
Electric tweezers are powered tweezers used to pluck brows, facial and stray body hair. Some versions are sold on the idea that an electrical signal at the tip damages the hair root, so hair stays away longer and brows or skin look cleaner.

The name covers a motorised gripping tool, and in hair removal, tweezers described as passing an electrical signal to the root. No human studies of the regrowth claim were found.
quick.how: Users grip and pluck individual hairs for brow shaping and stray-hair cleanup, as with ordinary tweezers. Plucking is repeated as hairs regrow.
quick.risks: No safety data were found for the electrified type. Skin irritation, redness and ingrown hairs are general plucking risks.

angle.text: Users pick electric tweezers to pluck brows, facial and stray body hair for a cleaner look. Some versions are sold on the idea that an electrical pulse damages the root so hair stays away longer. That regrowth claim has no human studies behind it.

braun-silk-expert-ipl.summary: Braun's home IPL hair-reduction device with a skin-tone sensor that adjusts or blocks flashes.

quick.overview:
Braun Silk-expert is a home intense pulsed light (IPL) line used for at-home hair reduction, with versions that use a skin-tone sensor to adjust or block flashes. The goal is less visible body hair over repeated sessions.

Pulsed light is absorbed by melanin in the hair and heats the follicle, so follicles weaken over multiple sessions. Home IPL as a category has trial support for hair reduction; trials specific to this line were not found.
quick.how: Users flash the device over shaved skin in sessions repeated over weeks, then do occasional maintenance. It works best on darker hair, and manufacturers restrict use to light-to-medium skin tones.
quick.risks: Burns, redness and pigmentation changes are reported with IPL, and light-based removal is limited by skin tone and hair colour. Eye safety is a design concern with home IPL.

angle.text: Users choose Braun Silk-expert IPL for at-home hair reduction. Light pulses target hair pigment and weaken follicles over repeated sessions, leaving less visible body hair. Home IPL has trial support as a category; trials specific to this line are not found.

philips-lumea.summary: Philips' handheld home IPL device for gradually reducing body and facial hair for smoother skin.

quick.overview:
The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) for long-term hair reduction at home, on the body and face, as an alternative to clinic treatment. The payoff is smoother, less hairy skin.

IPL flashes broad-spectrum light that is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating and damaging the follicle. Only hairs in the growth phase respond, so treatments are repeated over weeks. Clinical IPL generally reduces hair growth and is described as typically less effective than laser; evidence for this specific model is limited.
quick.how: Users flash the device over shaved skin in repeated sessions over weeks, then do occasional maintenance. It suits darker hair on lighter skin; light, grey, red and white hair respond poorly.
quick.risks: Reported risks of IPL include hyperpigmentation and eye injury if misused; a review of home IPL safety discussed the need for eye safety in consumer designs.

angle.text: The Philips Lumea is used at home for long-term hair reduction on the body and face. Pulsed light heats the follicles, so hair growth slows over sessions and skin looks smoother. Home IPL has some trial support for hair reduction; evidence for this model is limited.

tria-beauty-hair-removal-laser.summary: An at-home diode laser for longer-lasting hair reduction, one of two over-the-counter diode devices FDA-cleared as of 2025.

quick.overview:
The Tria is a consumer diode laser for hair removal at home, used for longer-lasting hair reduction than shaving provides. According to Wikipedia, it is one of two diode devices the US FDA had cleared for over-the-counter sale as of 2025, and the clearance covers hair reduction.

Laser energy is absorbed by melanin in the hair and heats the follicle, damaging it while sparing most surrounding skin (selective photothermolysis). Clinic laser hair removal is described as producing long-term reduction rather than total removal, usually needing several sessions.
quick.how: Users treat shaved skin in sessions repeated over weeks to months, then maintain as needed. Dark, coarse hair on lighter skin responds best.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, itching and swelling lasting a few days; burns, pigment changes and eye injury are possible. Light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly.

angle.text: Users buy the Tria as an at-home diode laser for longer-lasting hair reduction than shaving. Laser energy is absorbed by hair pigment and damages the follicles over repeated sessions. It is one of two over-the-counter diode lasers the FDA had cleared as of 2025, for hair reduction.

silk-n-infinity-flash-go.summary: Silk'n home light-based devices for gradual hair reduction; an early study of the brand's home pulsed light device reported hair reduction.

quick.overview:
Silk'n makes home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go lines, used for gradual hair reduction and smoother, less hairy skin. They use low-energy pulsed light designed for self-treatment.

Home pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin and heats the follicle, so hair thins across sessions. A 2009 study of an early Silk'n home device tested 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts and reported hair reduction; the Infinity and Flash&Go models themselves have no trial in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: Users flash the device over shaved skin in repeated sessions over weeks, then maintain occasionally. Home IPL suits darker hair on lighter skin.
quick.risks: A 2010 review of home IPL devices noted they are designed to damage follicles, with eye safety a key design concern. Home-use IPL is generally considered less suited to very dark skin or light hair.

angle.text: Users apply Silk'n Infinity and Flash&Go devices at home for gradual hair reduction. Home pulsed light hits the follicles, so hair thins across sessions and skin looks smoother. A small 2009 study of an early Silk'n device reported hair reduction; the current models are less studied.
